key_insight: Vision–language models' weak reasoning stems largely from reporting bias in their caption-based training data: people omit tacit visual facts in natural captions, and simply scaling models or data does not recover the missing supervision needed for certain kinds of visual reasoning.
problem_solved: Explains why state-of-the-art VLMs continue to fail on some reasoning tasks despite scale — identifying reporting bias in web-harvested captions as a fundamental barrier and empirically showing that larger scale alone cannot overcome it.
method: Quantitative analysis of large image–caption corpora (e.g., datasets used to train OpenCLIP) to measure how often captions omit concrete visual facts (reporting bias).
Design of evaluation tasks that require tacit visual information (e.g., counts, explicit attributes, relational facts) to reveal reasoning failures across model sizes.

Empirical experiments comparing model performance across scales and testing simple data interventions (e.g., targeted supervision or augmented literal captions) to assess whether fixing labels helps more than scaling.
impact: Shows that dataset pragmatics, not just model capacity, limit VLM reasoning — so practitioners should prioritize curated supervision, targeted annotations, or synthetic/literal captioning strategies when building VLMs rather than relying only on scale.
visual_elements: Side-by-side caption examples: natural/reporting caption vs. literal/detail-rich caption (e.g., "at the game today!" vs. "37 people standing behind a field").
Bar chart: model reasoning performance vs. model/data scale, illustrating performance plateau despite increased scale.
Heatmap or table: frequency of omitted visual facts in training corpora (types of tacit info like counts, colors, relations).
Schematic before/after: baseline VLM trained on raw captions vs. VLM with targeted supervision showing improved answers on reasoning tasks.
paper_title: Scale Can't Overcome Pragmatics: The Impact of Reporting Bias on Vision-Language Reasoning
paper_authors: Amita Kamath, Jack Hessel, Khyathi Chandu, Jena D. Hwang, Kai-Wei Chang
